🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -0.69% (intraday, 7-year +10bp). The pre-market story is a broad move into bonds and out of oil. WTI is down 3.42 to 89.45 (-3.68%) and Brent is down 2.64 to 99.67. Yields are falling everywhere: the US 10Y is at 5.1675 (-7.32bp), the 2Y at 4.7246 (-6.68bp), the Bund 10Y at 3.387 (-12.1bp) and the Gilt 10Y at 5.301 (-9.7bp). US futures are higher: ES +64.5 to 7788.5, NQ +356.5 to 31117 and Dow futures +443 to 51684. Yesterday's cash session closed slightly up (S&P 500 7666.45, +0.19%; Russell 2000 +0.35%), and the VIX fell to 15.53 from 16.39. Europe is extending the move (Euro Stoxx 50 +0.73%, STOXX 600 +0.71%), while the Nikkei closed down 0.94%. The moves line up with the Iran headlines: talks have stalled and a tanker was attacked in Hormuz, but Trump says Iran is 'ready to fold up' (CBS). That causal link is our reading, not a confirmed driver. Gold is up 1.06% to 4221.97 even in a risk-on tape, which suggests investors are still holding hedges. Sentiment is constructive but fragile. The 10Y is still more than 5%, the Fed has just started hiking again, and US indexes sit at the top of their historical range (computed). We read this as a relief rally, not a change of regime.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 451.11 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is trading at 451.11 cents/gal, at the 99.7th percentile with a z-score of 2.98, and every stretch measure on the board is at a historical extreme. Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

US sectors over 1 day are led by Energy (+1.92), Industrials (+1.00), Info Tech (+0.76) and Utilities (+0.61). Health Care (-1.30) and Comm Services (-1.19) lag. Over 1 month, Info Tech (+6.28) and Comm Services (+3.57) are the only gainers. Real Estate (-7.18), Utilities (-6.36), Financials (-6.31) and Materials (-6.07) were hit hardest, the signature of a rising-rate shock that punishes rate-sensitive defensives and banks. YTD, Energy (+37.20) and Info Tech (+28.76) dominate, while Utilities (-8.17) and Cons Discr (-5.35) trail. Global sectors rhyme: Info Tech is +36.18 YTD and Energy +31.75, while Materials (-8.25 1m) and Financials (-6.23 1m) are weak. The defensives (Staples, Health Care, Utilities, Real Estate) are all negative over the month on both screens. So rates, not growth fear, are driving rotation: duration-sensitive defensives are being sold, and the market is concentrated in tech growth plus the energy/war trade. If today's yield drop lasts, the oversold rate-sensitives (Real Estate, Utilities) are the natural catch-up candidates.

Widening velocity, not level. The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. 💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +1.01 vol points (76th percentile of the 33 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 108.1 (78th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 115bp (steeper by 43bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (99bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.28 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 58/100 — Core inflation is moderately persistent and easing at the margin. Every computed underlying measure (median, trimmed-mean, sticky) is flagged 'falling', and they cluster near 2.2-2.7%, around mid-history percentiles. Headline-sensitive pressure still runs hot: Flexible CPI is 4.94 and the 1y breakeven of 2.6843 is above the 5y at 2.3553. Breadth is split. In the Dallas distribution, 28.9% of the basket (13.2% above 10% plus 15.7% at 5-10%) is rising fast, while 25.8% is falling, and the biggest bucket is 2-3% (27.4%). Core PCE at 3.00759 is still well above target, which explains the Fed's September hike. Lower oil today helps the flexible component. Overall: sticky but not re-accelerating.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The current Nasdaq path since the Oct-2022 low (index 244.6 after 48 months) roughly matches the early-to-mid run of the 1990s analogs, not the parabolic 1998-2000 leg. The computed valuation marker sits at 22% of the way to the peak P/E. The risk is not a 2000-style valuation blow-off. It is that tight credit and low volatility coexist with a hiking Fed and a 5%+ 10Y. In 2000, the trigger was the Fed tightening into froth, and the 1999-2000 hikes preceded a -78% Nasdaq drawdown over 31 months (computed). The five analyst-estimate inputs (top-10 concentration ~40%, IPO froth ~45, CAPE ~39x, market cap/GDP ~215%, long-term EPS-growth expectations ~65) are approximate judgments and were not web-verified this run. Treat them as indicative. Oura's oversubscribed listing (about 4x demand, per channelnews) is a sign of healthy, not manic, IPO appetite.

⚔️Iran War

The US-Israel war with Iran, under way since 28 February 2026, is in a tense diplomatic stalemate with continued attacks at sea. After talks stalled, Secretary of State Rubio demanded the Iranian UN General Assembly delegation leave the US immediately. Trump said Iran is 'ready to fold up' and that the US will win 'right after the election.' He told TIME that military action could resume after the midterms without a satisfactory deal. A tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz (crew reported safe, damage unknown), and Trump said he believes Iran was behind the drone attack that shut the Saudi East-West pipeline (all per CBS live updates). Market read, our inference: today's 3.68% WTI drop suggests traders are pricing an eventual deal, or at least no further escalation before the midterms. Shipping and pipeline attacks keep upside oil-price tail risk alive.

Sources: Trump says Iran "ready to fold up," after threatening post-midterm attacks (CBS News) · 2026 Iran war (Wikipedia) · Early Edition: October 1, 2026 (Just Security)

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Next meeting: close call between a hold and another 25bp hike, with a slight lean to a hike if core PCE stays near 3%. After the September presser, CME FedWatch priced a 49% chance of an October hike, and 16 of 19 FOMC members projected at least one more hike this year (cited). Our inference: the weak payroll print (29k), falling oil and today's drop in yields give doves room to argue for a pause.

~1 YEAR

Inferred from Warsh's on-record emphasis on a 'timelier return' to 2% and a 'quieter' Fed: policy stays restrictive, with funds likely peaking around 4.00-4.25% (analyst estimate) before any cuts in H2 2027 once core PCE converges. Expect less forward guidance and fewer Fed speeches. Balance-sheet reduction is likely to remain a preferred tool, an inference from his long-standing views that we did not verify this run.

The Fed held in June at Warsh's first meeting. In September it hiked 25bp, unanimously, to 3.75%-4.00%, its first increase since 2023, as Warsh vowed a 'timelier return' to 2% inflation. At Jackson Hole he stressed concern about inflation and advocated a 'quieter' central bank (CNBC). He is a hawk who prefers to act rather than talk. The data support that bias on core PCE (3.00759), but the labor market (NFP 29) is the counterweight. Points labeled as inference are our reading, not reported fact.
